title: Global Power Is Shifting. How Can Leaders Adapt?
gist: BCG's new Power Index scores nations on 52 indicators across economic (45%), military (30%) and soft power (25%), and finds the world is not yet truly multipolar: the US leads with a composite 19 in 2025 versus China at 14 and a coordinated Europe at 13, with Russia (4) and India (3) below the pole threshold. The decisive variable is now alliance configuration, not organic national growth — a US-Europe bloc scores 32 versus China's 14, while a China-Russia bloc (18) would nearly match a go-it-alone US (19). The corporate implication is that exposure should be measured by domain (chips, critical mineral processing, digital infrastructure, financial plumbing) rather than by country.

themes.theme: Power Index methodology and the pole threshold

insights.claim: BCG's Power Index scores nations 0-100 across 52 indicators in three dimensions weighted economic 45%, military 30%, and soft power 25%, with technology and governance treated as enablers rather than standalone dimensions.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Gives investors a reproducible, weight-adjustable scoreboard for geopolitical risk instead of narrative-driven country ratings; the weights are explicitly tunable, so stress-test conclusions under a heavier military weighting.
insights.quote: Economic power in our composite index is weighted at 45%, military power at 30%, and soft power at 25%. This is a qualitative judgement on our part and is easily adjusted in our proprietary model.
insights.locator: Our Methodology — Weighting

insights.claim: The higher 45% weight on economic power is justified because technological production inputs — AI, semiconductors and quantum computing leadership — sit inside the economic dimension and cascade downstream into military capability and soft power projection.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Implies chip and AI leadership is the master variable for national power — the same assets investors track for earnings are being repriced as strategic assets subject to state control.
insights.locator: The higher economic weight reflects the inclusion

insights.claim: A 'pole' is defined operationally as any state, empire or coordinated bloc scoring 10+ on the composite index or 15+ in any single dimension — a deliberately higher bar than academic definitions such as controlling 5%-10% of global military power.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The threshold is what makes 'multipolarity' falsifiable; using a lower academic bar would classify Russia and India as poles and materially change scenario analysis.
insights.quote: This threshold sets a “great power” threshold that is higher than in some academic literature
insights.locator: Defining Poles

insights.claim: The pole threshold was back-tested against two consensus historical cases: in 1939 it admits the USSR, US, British Empire and Third Reich while excluding France and Japan, and for 1946-1990 it admits only the US and USSR while excluding China in 1970.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Validation against known-multipolar and known-bipolar eras is the credibility test for the index; it means the 'not yet multipolar' verdict is a methodological output, not an opinion.
insights.locator: We validated this threshold against two periods

insights.claim: The index's own periodization dates the current era of 'emerging alternatives' from 2014, anchored on China's Belt and Road launch, the deterioration of US-China trade and political relations, and Russia's annexation of Crimea.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Sets 2014, not 2016 or 2020, as the structural break — useful for choosing regime-change dates when backtesting geopolitical risk premia.
insights.locator: 2014–present: Emerging alternatives

insights.claim: Governance quality is a power enabler because historically most great powers declined from internal dynamics — regime change or collapse driven by corruption, poor planning and inability to adapt — rather than from foreign invasion and occupation.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Argues domestic institutional decay, not military defeat, is the leading indicator of a power's decline — a reason to watch internal political stability metrics as much as defense budgets.
insights.quote: Throughout history, many countries and empires have fallen not because another power invaded their territory, seized their capital, and took charge.
insights.locator: Governance. Strong and stable governance

themes.theme: The 2025 scorecard: no single dominant power

insights.claim: As of 2025 the US leads the composite index with a score of 19 while China ranks second at 14, but neither leads across all three power dimensions, forcing both to rely on allies to achieve global strategic aims.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Quantifies the US-China gap as roughly 5 index points and frames alliance-building — not unilateral capability — as the swing factor for market access and supply chain rules.
insights.quote: The US remains on top, with a composite score of 19 in 2025, but China, in second position, has rapidly gained ground, with a score of 14.
insights.locator: Where the World Order Stands Now

insights.claim: The world today is more multipolar than at any time since before World War II but still falls short of true multipolarity, meaning the 'unipolar moment' in which today's incumbent leaders were formed is over even though no replacement structure has settled.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A contrarian correction to the casual 'we live in a multipolar world' consensus — the transition is incomplete, so the distribution of outcomes is wider than either a stable US-led or stable multipolar assumption implies.
insights.quote: While we may not be in a truly multipolar world at present, the “unipolar moment”—in which so many of our current leaders came of age—is clearly over.
insights.locator: Adapting to a Multipolar World

insights.claim: Commercial openness from the post-Cold War era is actively eroding as tariff and non-tariff barriers proliferate along three new axes — geography, technology, and company origin — fragmenting markets in ways not seen in decades.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Company-of-origin barriers, not just country barriers, mean corporate domicile itself becomes a risk factor — relevant to where multinationals incorporate, list, and locate IP.
insights.quote: Tariff and non-tariff barriers are proliferating based on geography, technology, and company origin, fragmenting the commercial landscape in ways not seen in decades.
insights.locator: Where the World Order Stands Now

insights.claim: The peak of commercial freedom was the unipolar period around 2000, when the US scored 23 on the composite index and firms could buy, manufacture and sell anywhere with limited government-imposed trade and technology restrictions.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The US has fallen from 23 to 19 in 25 years — a quantified measure of how much of the globalization dividend embedded in multinational margins has already eroded.
insights.quote: For business, this period of globalization was the high point of capitalist freedom: firms could buy, manufacture, and sell wherever they wanted with limited government-imposed trade and technology restrictions.
insights.locator: By 2000, the world was unmistakably unipolar

insights.claim: In 1914 the leading power scored only 15 (British Empire), followed by the US at 14, the Russian Empire at 11 and the German Empire at 10 — a distribution in which no pole dominated all three dimensions, closely resembling today's spread.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The nearest historical analogue to today's scoreboard is 1914, an era that resolved through war and map-redrawing — an uncomfortable base rate for tail-risk pricing.
insights.locator: In 1914, before the onset of World War I

insights.claim: In 1939 the US dominated economically with 25% of global GDP while the Third Reich dominated militarily with 36% of global military spending, showing that concentrated economic and military leadership can sit in rival states simultaneously.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A historical template for today's split — China leading manufacturing while the US leads force projection — and a reminder that such splits have previously been unstable.
insights.locator: In 1939, global power was even more tightly contested

insights.claim: During the Cold War the US and USSR each accounted for around 30% of global military spending for several decades, and that bipolar order segmented the world economy into Western and Eastern blocs with sharply limited commercial exchange.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Provides the concrete precedent for what bloc-segmentation does to trade volumes — the downside case if today's configurations harden.
insights.locator: After World War II and throughout the Cold War

themes.theme: US structural advantages: dollar, bases, platforms

insights.claim: The US dollar's roughly 60% share of global foreign reserves is a durable source of financial power that lets Washington control international payments systems and shape specific geopolitical outcomes through economic and financial sanctions.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Sanctions capacity is a function of reserve share — watch reserve composition data as the leading indicator of whether US financial coercion is losing bite.
insights.quote: the use of the US dollar as a global reserve currency, which has accounted for around 60% of global foreign reserves, has been a durable source of global US financial power
insights.locator: The US. As a global economic power

insights.claim: The US is roughly twice as militarily powerful as China on the index, with its edge concentrated in force projection via an unmatched global network of bases, nuclear capabilities, and alliances across Asia, the Middle East and Europe.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The US military premium is embedded in alliance and basing access rather than hardware alone, so any erosion of alliances degrades US military power faster than a budget cut would.
insights.locator: From a military perspective, the US is roughly twice

insights.claim: US soft power rests on three specific assets — the world's most extensive alliance network, universities attracting more international students than any single country, and US-based digital platforms with near-global dominance of online discourse.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Names international student flows and platform reach as measurable, policy-sensitive components of national power — immigration and platform-regulation shocks are geopolitical events, not just sector news.
insights.locator: On soft power, the US remains highly influential

insights.claim: The US dominates advanced semiconductor design and leads AI, and although quantum computing is early-stage the US leads in quantum investment and patents, giving it potential to disrupt cryptography and materials science.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Frames quantum as a strategic option position rather than a current capability — investment and patent share are the observable leading indicators to track.
insights.locator: Technologically, the US dominates advanced semiconductor design

themes.theme: China's asymmetric position and the renminbi ceiling

insights.claim: China controls 60% to 90% of global processing capacity for metals and minerals critical to the energy transition, defense manufacturing and consumer electronics.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The single most concentrated chokepoint in the report — processing, not reserves, is the bottleneck, so Western mining capex without refining capacity does not reduce exposure.
insights.quote: China also controls 60% to 90% of processing capacity for metals and minerals that are critical to energy transition, defense manufacturing, and consumer electronics.
insights.locator: China. Our index ranks China roughly tied

insights.claim: The renminbi accounts for only about 2% of international reserves, and meaningful internationalization would require China to open its capital account and make the currency convertible — domestic risks Beijing has so far been unwilling to accept.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Places a hard political ceiling on de-dollarization narratives: without capital-account liberalization the RMB cannot displace the dollar, so watch convertibility policy, not bilateral trade settlement headlines.
insights.quote: the renminbi remains far from being a global reserve currency, reflecting only about 2% of international reserves
insights.locator: However, the renminbi remains far

insights.claim: China holds a dominant share of global manufacturing and goods exports concentrated in EVs, batteries and renewable energy systems, and is the only major competitor to the US in frontier AI models.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Identifies the four sectors where Chinese export dominance is most likely to trigger Western trade barriers — EVs, batteries, renewables, and AI models.
insights.locator: It has a dominant share of global manufacturing

insights.claim: China spends around half as much on its military as the US and lacks the overseas bases and alliances required for global force projection, making it a regional superpower rather than a global military pole.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Suggests Chinese military risk should be priced regionally (Indo-Pacific shipping, Taiwan-adjacent supply chains) rather than as a global security threat.
insights.quote: But it is a superpower in its region.
insights.locator: In the defense domain, China spends around half

insights.claim: China converts financial resources into soft power principally through Belt and Road infrastructure lending and through its e-commerce and social media platforms, which generate significant global cultural influence.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Chinese consumer platforms are treated as instruments of state influence in this framework, which is precisely the logic driving Western platform bans and forced divestitures.
insights.locator: And in terms of soft power, China has leveraged

themes.theme: Europe's coordination premium and its limits

insights.claim: Europe defined as the EU-27 plus the UK and the four EFTA members scores 13 as a coordinated bloc, but Germany, the UK and France each score only 2 individually — behind Russia, Japan and India.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Quantifies the coordination premium at roughly 13 versus 2 — European policy cohesion is worth more than any single member's capability, so fragmentation risk is the key European variable.
insights.quote: Taken alone, Germany, the UK, and France, for example, each have composite scores of 2, behind Russia, Japan, and India.
insights.locator: Europe. When the countries we include

insights.claim: Europe leads all poles in soft power on the strength of institutional maturity, development assistance, diplomatic networks and cultural reach, and is the world's largest consumer market, yet still trails the US and China economically.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Europe's leverage is regulatory and market-access based rather than economic or military — the Brussels effect is its real export.
insights.locator: Europe leads all other poles in soft power

insights.claim: The euro holds around 20% of global reserves but Eurozone countries lack an integrated fiscal policy to match the ECB's unified monetary policy, capping the euro's ability to compete with the dollar.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Names fiscal integration — joint issuance and a common safe asset — as the specific precondition for the euro gaining reserve share; watch EU fiscal union proposals as the trigger.
insights.quote: The euro accounts for around 20% of the world’s reserves, but the Eurozone countries do not have an integrated fiscal policy to match the ECB’s unified monetary policy.
insights.locator: Although an integrated Europe is the world’s largest consumer market

insights.claim: A combined Europe excluding the US, Canada and Türkiye is roughly on par with China militarily and slightly stronger than Russia, but deploying that capability requires political consensus across many governments — a constraint neither Russia nor China faces.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: European military capability on paper exceeds the usual perception, but the binding constraint is decision speed, not hardware — favoring investment in command integration over pure equipment spend.
insights.quote: However, deploying its military capability requires political consensus among many governments, a constraint neither Russia nor China face.
insights.locator: Militarily, a combined Europe

insights.claim: Europe is no longer as closely aligned with the US as it was in the unipolar period around 2000, when it was clearly strategically aligned militarily, economically and culturally.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The transatlantic alignment that produced the strongest possible pole (score 32) is treated as eroding, raising the probability weight on the less favorable configurations.
insights.quote: The region, however, is no longer as closely aligned with the US.
insights.locator: Europe—defined here as the 27 members

insights.claim: Russia scores only 4 on the composite index and does not qualify as a pole, but holds nearly half the world's deployed strategic nuclear warheads and a 1.3-million-strong standing military, with energy exports providing leverage across Eastern Europe and South Asia.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Russia is a narrow-spectrum power — nuclear and energy leverage on a weakened, sanctions-hit economic base — so its influence is concentrated in escalation risk and energy pricing rather than broad economic competition.
insights.quote: Its nuclear arsenal accounts for nearly half of the world’s deployed strategic warheads, and its 1.3-million-strong standing military gives it formidable conventional capability in its region.
insights.locator: Russia. Although Russia doesn’t meet

insights.claim: India scores 3 today but is identified as the power with the greatest potential to become a pole, combining the world's largest population, a fast-growing economy and technical talent with deliberate strategic flexibility — Quad membership since 2007 alongside enduring Russian defense and energy ties.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: India is the highest-optionality geopolitical position in the index; its alignment choice is a swing factor investors should track as a discrete event risk for supply chain relocation flows.
insights.quote: With a composite score of 3, India is not yet a pole but is arguably the power with the greatest potential to become one.
insights.locator: India. With a composite score of 3

insights.claim: Japan ranks highest among the second tier of powers, with global reach disproportionate to its composite score driven by the world's third-largest economy, extensive foreign assistance programs and its diplomatic network.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Japan's influence is soft-power and capital-flow based, making it a disproportionately valuable partner in any bloc scenario relative to its raw score.
insights.locator: Japan scores highest among this group

insights.claim: South Korea ranks sixth globally on the military index with substantial warship and armored-vehicle inventories, on top of a strong semiconductor, consumer electronics and heavy industrial base.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: South Korea combines chip supply criticality with genuine defense-industrial scale — a dual exposure that makes it both a target and a beneficiary of bloc formation.
insights.locator: South Korea is a major advanced manufacturing economy

insights.claim: Canada's power derives from vast hydrocarbon and renewable energy endowments, coastlines on three oceans, status as a top destination for international students, and significant R&D investment.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Positions Canada as an energy-and-talent play whose strategic value rises if North American bloc integration deepens.
insights.locator: Canada has vast energy endowments

insights.claim: Australia holds significant reserves of critical minerals including lithium and rare earths while serving as a key US defense partner in the Indo-Pacific, and Türkiye derives power from controlling the Bosphorus chokepoint plus a large, well-equipped military.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Australia is the most credible non-Chinese source of critical minerals and Türkiye the key maritime chokepoint holder — both are structural beneficiaries of supply-chain and transit derisking.
insights.locator: Australia occupies a strategic position

insights.claim: Outside the top ten, Indonesia, Nigeria, Brazil and Saudi Arabia are singled out as considerable powers capable of playing critical roles regionally and globally despite divergent economic, military and soft power trajectories.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Flags the next cohort of swing states whose alignment can be courted — relevant to frontier and EM allocation as bloc-building intensifies.
insights.locator: Outside of the top ten

insights.claim: Alliances can broaden, deepen and amplify power projection far faster than any single power can strengthen or weaken through organic growth or decline, making alliance configuration the dominant near-term variable in global power.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Diplomatic events, not GDP trends, are the fast-moving driver of geopolitical repricing — treat summit outcomes and defense-pact changes as material catalysts.
insights.quote: These alliances can broaden, deepen, and amplify the projection of power much more quickly than any single power can strengthen or weaken through organic growth or decline.
insights.locator: The index also reveals the crucial role

insights.claim: A formally aligned US and Europe would score 32 versus China's 14 and would dominate every dimension, running roughly three times more powerful than China in both military and soft power.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The transatlantic bloc is by far the strongest available configuration — a concrete argument that US-EU friction is the most value-destructive geopolitical development for the West.
insights.locator: Configuration 1: US and Europe are formally aligned

insights.claim: A China-Russia pole would score 18, only slightly below a standalone US at 19, and would hold more economic power than the US while lagging on military capability and soft power.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Transatlantic decoupling plus Sino-Russian alignment produces near-parity — the specific scenario in which US sanctions and market-access leverage stop working reliably.
insights.quote: A pole consisting of China and Russia, with a composite score of 18, would be only slightly less powerful than the US on its own and far more powerful than a unified Europe.
insights.locator: Configuration 2: China and Russia are aligned

insights.claim: A bloc of US mutual-defense treaty allies excluding the US itself — NATO members plus Australia, Japan, South Korea and the Philippines — would score 22, making it stronger than both a standalone US (19) and a combined China-Russia (18).
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The most counterintuitive finding in the report: America's allies without America would be the strongest single pole, which reframes US alliance withdrawal as self-weakening rather than ally-weakening.
insights.quote: As such, it would be slightly more powerful than the US and a unified China and Russia, with composite scores of 19 and 18, respectively.
insights.locator: Configuration 3: China and Russia remain aligned

insights.claim: Decades-old alignments are eroding into transactional relationships, so alliance configurations now shift frequently and their futures are harder to predict than at any point in the post-war era.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Higher variance in alliance structure argues for scenario-weighted rather than point-forecast planning and for a persistent geopolitical risk premium in globally exposed assets.
insights.quote: But as decades-old alignments now erode and become more transactional, the configurations of such alliances frequently shift, and their futures are harder to predict.
insights.locator: How Alliances Redefine the Power Balance

insights.claim: Under a China-Russia versus decoupled-West configuration, India, Japan, South Korea, Türkiye, Brazil, Saudi Arabia and Indonesia would carry disproportionate weight in trade, technology policy, security cooperation and regional issues despite trailing the poles in all three dimensions.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific seven middle powers whose bargaining power — and ability to extract investment, technology transfer and security guarantees — rises most in a fractured world.
insights.locator: As potential allies, India, Japan, South Korea

themes.theme: Corporate playbook: domain exposure over country exposure

insights.claim: Traditional country-level geopolitical risk assessment is becoming obsolete; exposure to blocs and to specific domains — semiconductor supply chains, critical mineral processing, digital infrastructure and financial architecture — may matter more than exposure to any single country.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A directly actionable reframe: map portfolio and supplier exposure by chokepoint domain rather than by country of operation, since a firm dependent on specific chip or rare-earth facilities carries concentrated risk regardless of its headquarters.
insights.quote: Assess exposure by domain, not just geography.
insights.locator: Assess exposure by domain

insights.claim: Shifts in the levers of power are usually visible before they become decisive but appear as weak signals that are easy to dismiss, so leaders should track emerging concentrations in AI, quantum computing research, critical mineral processing and new materials as leading indicators of where leverage will move next.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Names four specific watchlist domains where capability concentration precedes geopolitical leverage — a concrete screen for early positioning.
insights.quote: The historical record shows that shifts in the levers of power are often visible before they become decisive.
insights.locator: Monitor where new concentrations of capability are forming

insights.claim: Policy responses to polarity shifts can be abrupt: trade routes open for decades can close within months or even days, routine technology partnerships can become restricted, and supply chains optimized for efficiency can become liabilities.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Argues efficiency-optimized supply chains carry unpriced tail risk with near-zero warning time — a case for paying up for redundancy and dual-sourcing before, not after, a shock.
insights.quote: Trade routes that were open for decades can close within months or even days.
insights.locator: History has shown that when polarity shifts

insights.claim: Understanding a firm's dependence on foreign nations across purchasing, value-adding transformation and end markets has moved from being a compliance exercise to a core determinant of competitiveness.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Predicts geopolitical mapping becomes a strategy function rather than a legal one — expect governance and disclosure around it to expand, and to differentiate corporate performance.
insights.quote: is no longer merely a compliance exercise. It is essential to ensuring competitiveness in the years ahead.
insights.locator: Understanding the dependence of a firm’s operations

insights.claim: Past polarity shifts redistributed commercial advantage to the victors' national firms — after World War I, British, French and US companies gained preferential access to newly carved-out territories and markets as the map was redrawn.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Historical base rate that bloc realignment creates concentrated corporate winners tied to state alignment — national champions in the winning bloc capture rents, an argument for tracking political alignment as an equity factor.
insights.quote: British, French, and US firms gained preferential access to newly carved-out or created territories and markets.
insights.locator: The war that followed redrew the world map

insights.claim: Leaders should stress-test global strategy against multiple future power configurations, assessing how geopolitical realignment would change investment, sourcing, manufacturing, product development and global marketing decisions under each scenario.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Converts the index into a planning tool: measure exposure to each configuration rather than forecasting one, since the three modeled scenarios imply radically different market-access and tech-stack outcomes.
insights.locator: Stress-test global strategy against multiple future power configurations
